Field guide · start here
Getting started
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Sections 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 5.1
What every county employee needs in the first hour of an activation: how lifelines are rated, what the EOC level means for you, and how to report what you see.
EOC line
540-928-2265
Any issue during an activation
Lifeline status levels
EOP 3.4 · used in every SitRep
Stabilized · Green · Minimal impact
Functioning normally, re-established, or not impacted. Monitor.
Impacted · Yellow · Moderate impact
Working with workarounds, partly disrupted, or at risk. Active monitoring; put contingencies in place.
Destabilized · Red · Significant impact
Failed or severely disrupted. Priority resources; escalate.
Not assessed · Gray
No report yet from the lifeline lead. Ask the lead for a status at the next briefing.
EOC activation levels
EOP 3.7
LEVEL 3
Monitoring
Coordinator of EM monitors conditions and shares situational awareness through routine channels; virtual tools on standby.
Who: Emergency Manager and select staff as needed · Examples: weather watch issued; developing regional event; planned event coordination
LEVEL 2
Partial Activation
Virtual EOC active with select lifeline lead representatives; physical site designated only if in-person coordination is warranted.
Who: Emergency Manager, lifeline leads, key department heads · Examples: weather warning; moderate flooding; significant power outage; multi-agency incident
LEVEL 1
Full Activation
All lifeline leads participate; full ICS; physical EOC designated when scale requires; state/federal coordination active.
Who: All lifeline leads, department heads, liaison officers, agency reps · Examples: major disaster; multiple lifelines disrupted; local emergency declared; MCI
Activation authority
•
Director of Emergency Management (County Administrator) or Coordinator of Emergency Management may authorize EOC activation
•
Coordinator of EM decides virtual vs. physical EOC and selects participating stakeholders
•
Most activations are virtual; the level may be adjusted as the situation evolves
•
Board of Supervisors declares and terminates a local emergency; the County Administrator may recommend a declaration
Operational priorities
In order · EOP 3.5
1
Life safety and security of responders and the public
2
Stabilize Community Lifelines, those with greatest life-safety impact first
3
Protect property and critical infrastructure
4
Protect the environment
5
Restore essential community services
6
Economic recovery and return to normalcy
Activation decision flow
1
Identify threat/incident and assess scope
EM Coordinator / On-duty IC
2
Determine activation level from lifeline impacts
EM Coordinator
3
Notify Director of Emergency Management
EM Coordinator
4
Authorize activation; decide virtual or physical
Director of EM / EM Coordinator
5
Notify selected stakeholders and lifeline leads
EM Coordinator
6
Start lifeline status tracking in this app
Planning Section / EM Coordinator
7
Begin situation reports to VDEM Region 6
EOC Manager
How to report from the field
1
Make sure you are safe
do not enter water, downed lines or unstable structures
2
Open the field report form for your role (Responder, Public or Dispatch)
or call the EOC line, 540-928-2265
3
Pick the report type, describe what you see, and attach photos
4
Your report shows up in Field reports on the SitReps page and on the Situation Map

Lifeline 1 of 8 · EOP section 9.1
Safety & Security
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.1
This annex establishes the framework for maintaining and restoring safety and security services in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses law enforcement, fire services, search and rescue, government service continuity, and community safety including flood control and protective actions.
Lead
Sheriff's Office (law enforcement); Fire & EMS (fire, EMS, rescue, EM)
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
Police, fire, EMS, rescue, evacuations and keeping county government running.
What do I do now?
  1. Confirm Incident Command is set up at the scene.
  2. With the Incident Commander, decide on protective actions: evacuate, shelter in place or close an area.
  3. Ask Dispatch and the PIO to alert the public through Everbridge.
Who do I call?
Sheriff's Office · Fire & EMS
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
911/dispatch experiences a partial system degradation (CAD slowdown, single tower/repeater outage); law enforcement or Fire & EMS response times exceed established standards in one or more response areas; OR a protective action (evacuation or shelter-in-place) is issued for any portion of the county.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
911/dispatch capability is lost or the PSAP must evacuate; patrol or Fire & EMS coverage cannot be maintained in an affected area even with mutual aid; an evacuation is not completed before life-threatening conditions arrive; OR simultaneous incidents exceed local search-and-rescue/EMS capacity.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
911/dispatch is restored to full or backup operating capability; patrol and response coverage is reestablished countywide (mutual aid acceptable); search and rescue operations transition from active search to recovery/support.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
Response times return to established standards; no open evacuation or shelter-in-place orders remain in effect; mutual aid resources are released.
Checklists
EOP actions by phase · tap the gold Open live checklist button to assign and check off tasks
Response · 8 actions
1
Activate EOC to appropriate level based on incident scope
2
Deploy law enforcement, fire, and EMS resources to incident area
3
Establish Incident Command or Unified Command at the scene
4
Implement protective actions including evacuations, shelter-in-place, or access control
5
Initiate search and rescue operations as needed
6
Coordinate with Dispatch for public notification through Everbridge and other systems
7
Establish perimeter security and traffic control
8
Request mutual aid as needed through established escalation path
Preparedness · 6 actions
1
Maintain staffing and readiness of career and volunteer fire, EMS, and law enforcement personnel
2
Conduct regular training and exercises including tabletop, functional, and full-scale exercises
3
Maintain and test virtual EOC coordination platforms, communications systems, and equipment
4
Coordinate school safety planning with Botetourt County Public Schools
5
Maintain flood warning monitoring capability and evacuation route planning for high-risk areas
6
Maintain mutual aid agreements with adjacent jurisdictions
Recovery · 5 actions
1
Maintain security in disaster-affected areas to prevent looting and ensure public safety
2
Conduct damage assessment of public safety facilities and equipment
3
Transition from emergency operations to normal service delivery
4
Support reentry of evacuated populations when conditions are safe
5
Conduct after-action review and document lessons learned
Stabilization targets
What “stabilized” means for this lifeline
◎
Continuous 911 service availability
◎
Law enforcement patrol and response capability maintained throughout the incident
◎
Fire & EMS response operational within established response time standards
◎
Virtual EOC coordination activated within one hour of decision to activate; physical EOC facility, if designated, functional within two hours
◎
Evacuation of threatened populations completed before life-threatening conditions develop
◎
Search and rescue operations initiated within one hour of report of missing/trapped persons
Lead & support agencies
Lead
Sheriff's Office (law enforcement); Fire & EMS (fire, EMS, rescue, EM)
Support
Emergency Communications (radio); Dispatch (Sheriff’s Office); Community Development (floodplain, code enforcement); Botetourt County Public Schools; VDEM Region 6; Virginia State Police
Dependencies
CommunicationsEnergyTransportation
Safety and security operations are highly dependent on the Communications Lifeline for dispatch and coordination, the Energy Lifeline for facility power and traffic signals, and the Transportation Lifeline for access to incident areas. Loss of communications systems directly degrades the ability to coordinate safety and security response.

Lifeline 2 of 8 · EOP section 9.2
Food, Water, Shelter
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.2
This annex establishes the framework for providing food, water, and shelter services to affected populations in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses food distribution, potable water supply, wastewater services, mass sheltering, and agricultural protection. Note: Potable water infrastructure and wastewater management are addressed separately under the Water Systems Lifeline (Section 9.8).
Lead
Department of Social Services; Western Virginia Water Authority, Town of Troutville, Town of Buchanan, Town of Fincastle, Aqua Virginia
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
Food, drinking water for people, mass shelters, pets and farm animals.
What do I do now?
  1. Decide whether a shelter is needed, and where.
  2. Send the shelter team and supplies; start registering people.
  3. Set up feeding with the Red Cross and Salvation Army.
Who do I call?
Department of Social Services · water providers (Western Virginia Water Authority, the towns, Aqua Virginia)
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
A shelter activation decision is made; a food or water distribution disruption affecting a portion of the county is identified; OR agricultural operations report livestock or crop protection needs.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
Shelters cannot open within the four-hour stabilization target or exceed planned capacity; mass feeding cannot be established within 12 hours; potable water distribution cannot be established within 12 hours for a disrupted area; OR special needs/functional access populations cannot be sheltered.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
Shelters are operating within capacity and registering evacuees; mass feeding operations are established; alternate potable water distribution points are operating.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
Sheltered population transitioned to temporary or permanent housing and shelters deactivated; food distribution restored through normal commercial channels.

Stabilization targets
What “stabilized” means for this lifeline
◎
Emergency shelters opened and receiving evacuees within four hours of activation decision
◎
Mass feeding operations available within 12 hours of shelter activation
◎
Potable water distribution established within 12 hours for areas with water system disruption
◎
Boil water advisories or alternative water supply communicated to affected populations within two hours of determination
◎
Pet-friendly sheltering options available or coordinated with animal care providers

Lead (Sheltering)
Department of Social Services
Lead (Water)
Western Virginia Water Authority, Town of Troutville, Town of Buchanan, Town of Fincastle, Aqua Virginia
Support

Dependencies
CommunicationsEnergyTransportationSafety and SecurityWater Systems
Food, Water, and Shelter operations depend heavily on the Transportation Lifeline for supply delivery and evacuee movement, the Energy Lifeline for facility power (shelters, water treatment), the Communications Lifeline for public notifications, and the Safety and Security Lifeline for shelter security. Power loss at shelter facilities can degrade this lifeline. Water supply disruptions are now addressed under the Water Systems Lifeline (Lifeline 8).

Lifeline 3 of 8 · EOP section 9.3
Health & Medical
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.3
This annex establishes the framework for maintaining and restoring health and medical services in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses medical care, public health, patient movement, medical supply chain, and fatality management.
Lead
Department of Fire & EMS; Carilion Clinic / LewisGale Medical Center
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
EMS, hospitals, public health, medical supplies and fatality management.
What do I do now?
  1. Check hospital capacity and diversion status.
  2. Set up patient treatment and transport.
  3. Request medical supplies through EOC Logistics.
Who do I call?
Fire & EMS · Carilion Clinic / LewisGale Medical Center
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
EMS call volume or transport times exceed normal capacity; a receiving hospital reports diversion status; OR a behavioral health support request is received following a critical incident.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
Hospital surge exceeds regional bed capacity and an alternate care facility must be established (24-hour target); the medical supply chain remains disrupted beyond the 48-hour resupply target; a mass fatality event requires Medical Examiner coordination; OR EMS/ambulance transport capacity is exhausted with mutual aid unavailable.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
Alternate care facility is operational and accepting overflow patients, or hospital diversion is lifted; EMS transport capacity is restored via mutual aid; fatality management operations are stabilized.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
Hospitals resume normal receiving status; EMS response and transport times return to standard; behavioral health support transitions to routine referral.

Stabilization targets
What “stabilized” means for this lifeline
◎
EMS response and transport operational throughout the incident
◎
Alternate care facility established within 24 hours if hospital surge exceeds capacity
◎
Behavioral health support available to responders within 24 hours of a critical incident
◎
Medical supply chain assessed and supplemented within 48 hours of disruption
◎
Fatality management operations coordinated with Medical Examiner within four hours of mass fatality event

Department of Fire & EMS
Lead (Hospital Care)
Carilion Clinic / LewisGale Medical Center

CommunicationsEnergyTransportationSafety and Security

Loss of transportation routes to regional hospitals directly threatens this lifeline.

Lifeline 4 of 8 · EOP section 9.4
Energy
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.4
This annex establishes the framework for coordinating energy service restoration and continuity in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses electrical power grid operations, backup power generation, and fuel supply management.
Lead
Botetourt County Emergency Management; Appalachian Power (AEP); Craig-Botetourt Electric Cooperative; Dominion Energy
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
Power outages, backup generators and fuel.
What do I do now?
  1. Get restoration estimates from the power companies.
  2. Send generators to priority facilities.
  3. If a long outage meets extreme heat or cold, open warming or cooling centers and start welfare checks.
Who do I call?
Emergency Management · Appalachian Power (AEP) · Craig-Botetourt Electric Cooperative · Dominion Energy
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
A utility provider reports an outage affecting any portion of the county with a restoration estimate beyond six hours; OR a critical facility (designated EOC facility, shelter, Emergency Communications) loses primary power.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
Critical facilities cannot be placed on backup power within the one-hour target; utility providers cannot provide restoration estimates within six hours; the outage affects a significant share of county customers with no defined restoration timeline; OR extreme temperatures combine with an extended outage and warming/cooling centers cannot open within the eight-hour target.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
Backup power is confirmed operating at all critical facilities; utility providers issue firm restoration timelines; warming/cooling centers are operational.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
Utility service is fully restored to affected areas; generators are demobilized; no vulnerable populations remain without power support.

4

5

6

7

1
Maintain and test generators available for backup generation
2
Maintain inventory of available portable generators and fuel supplies
3
Establish communication protocols with service provider emergency contacts
4
Identify critical facilities requiring priority power restoration
5
Develop and maintain fuel prioritization plan
6
Identify warming/cooling center locations with backup power capability
Recovery · 5 actions
1
Monitor full power restoration and assist with information to affected areas
2
Demobilize generators and replenish fuel supplies
3
Coordinate with utilities for infrastructure hardening and mitigation measures
4
Document costs and damage for reimbursement
5
Conduct after-action review of energy coordination operations
Stabilization targets
What “stabilized” means for this lifeline
◎
Critical county facilities (Emergency Communications, designated EOC facility when activated, shelters) on backup power within one hour of outage
◎
Utility companies provide estimated restoration times within six hours of outage
◎
Generator deployment to priority facilities within four hours of request
◎
Warming/cooling centers operational within eight hours of extended power outage during extreme temperatures
◎
Fuel prioritization plan activated when supply disruptions threaten emergency operations
Lead & support agencies
Lead (Coordination)
Botetourt County Emergency Management
Lead (Operations)
Appalachian Power (AEP); Craig-Botetourt Electric Cooperative; Dominion Energy
Support
Department of Fire & EMS; Information Technology; Maintenance Department; VDEM Region 6

CommunicationsTransportationHealth and MedicalSafety and Security
Energy lifeline operations are dependent on the Transportation Lifeline for utility crew access and fuel delivery, the Communications Lifeline for coordination between the county and utility providers, and the Safety and Security Lifeline for traffic control and scene safety at damaged power infrastructure. Energy disruptions cascade rapidly to affect all other lifelines, particularly Communications, Health and Medical, Food/Water/Shelter, and Safety and Security.

Lifeline 5 of 8 · EOP section 9.5
Communications
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.5
This annex establishes the framework for maintaining and restoring communications services in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses telecommunications infrastructure, responder communications, public alerts and warnings, 911/dispatch operations, and financial services communications.
Lead
Emergency Communications (radio system); Dispatch (Sheriff’s Office); Information Technology (networks/systems)
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
911 and dispatch, responder radios, phone and internet, and public alerts.
What do I do now?
  1. Confirm 911 and dispatch are working.
  2. Add radio channels or switch to backup systems if needed.
  3. Get public alerts out through Everbridge and county channels.
Who do I call?
Emergency Communications · Dispatch (Sheriff’s Office) · Information Technology
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
A radio dead zone, tower, or repeater failure degrades responder communications; the Everbridge mass notification system experiences a partial failure; OR the county website/social media cannot be updated within the one-hour target.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
911/PSAP operations are lost or must transfer to a backup or mutual aid dispatch center; primary and backup communications systems both fail; OR responder radio communications cannot be restored within the one-hour target.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
911/PSAP operations are restored (primary or backup); responder radio communications are restored; public notification capability is reestablished.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
All primary communications systems (radio, telephone, data, notification) are restored to full capability; backup systems are demobilized.

2

Maintain and regularly test all communications systems including radio, telephone, and data networks
2

3
Test Everbridge mass notification system quarterly
4
Train personnel on backup communications procedures
5
Maintain media contact lists and Joint Information Center procedures
6
Identify and address radio coverage gaps throughout the county
7

1
Restore all communications systems to full operational capability
2
Demobilize deployed communications equipment and replenish supplies
3
Continue public information operations through recovery phase
4
Conduct assessment of communications system performance during the incident

Stabilization targets
What “stabilized” means for this lifeline
◎
Continuous 911 operations throughout the incident (zero downtime goal)
◎
Responder radio communications maintained or restored within one hour of disruption
◎
First public notification issued within one hour of significant incident
◎
County website and social media updated within one hour of significant incident
◎
Backup communications systems operational within one hour of primary system failure
Lead & support agencies
Lead
Emergency Communications (radio system); Dispatch (Sheriff’s Office); Information Technology (networks/systems)
Support
Office of Communications (public information); Department of Fire & EMS; Sheriff's Office; VDEM Region 6
Dependencies
EnergyTransportation
Communications lifeline operations are dependent on the Energy Lifeline for power to communications facilities, towers, and equipment. Loss of power is the most common cause of communications system degradation. The Transportation Lifeline affects the ability to deploy repair crews and equipment. Communications is foundational to all other lifelines — degradation of communications cascades to affect every other lifeline.

Lifeline 6 of 8 · EOP section 9.6
Transportation
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Section 9.6
This annex establishes the framework for maintaining and restoring transportation systems in Botetourt County during emergencies. It addresses highway and roadway systems, mass transit, railway operations, and aviation.
Lead
Virginia Department of Transportation (VDOT); Department of Fire & EMS
Start here · three questions
What does this cover?
Roads, I-81, rail, aviation and evacuation routes.
What do I do now?
  1. Close unsafe roads and set detours.
  2. Work with VDOT to clear and repair roads.
  3. Keep evacuation routes open; send road conditions for public alerts.
Who do I call?
VDOT · Fire & EMS
Numbers are on Key contacts. EOC line: 540-928-2265.
Report my lifeline status The full checklist, triggers and details are below.
Status change triggers
When to change this lifeline’s status (report it with Update my lifeline)
GREEN→YELLOWESCALATE
A primary or evacuation route is closed or impassable (flooding, downed trees, incident); an I-81 incident requires active traffic management; OR a community becomes isolated with a viable alternate route still available.
YELLOW→REDESCALATE
Primary evacuation routes cannot be cleared within the four-hour target; a community is isolated with no viable alternate access; the I-81 traffic incident management plan cannot be implemented within one hour of a major incident; OR emergency vehicle access cannot be maintained or re-routed to an occupied area.
RED→YELLOWSTEP DOWN
Alternate emergency access is established to all occupied areas even if primary routes remain closed; I-81 traffic management is operating effectively.
YELLOW→GREENSTEP DOWN
All primary routes and evacuation routes are reopened; bridge and road safety assessments are completed and cleared; normal traffic patterns are restored.
Checklists
EOP actions by phase · tap the gold Open live checklist button to assign and check off tasks

Flooding and Flash Flooding · EOP 10.1
Lead agency
Department of Fire & EMS
Trigger conditions
National Weather Service issues Flood Warning, or Flash Flood Warning for Botetourt County; river gauges on James River, Craig Creek, Catawba Creek, or Tinker Creek reach flood stage; reports of road flooding or structure inundation.
Lifelines most impacted
Transportation (road closures, bridge impacts); Safety and Security (evacuation, swift water rescue); Food, Water, Shelter (displacement); Energy (substation flooding); Water Systems (water contamination, treatment plant flooding).
Key initial actions
1
Activate EOC monitoring; assign personnel to monitor river gauges and NWS products
2
Pre-position swift water rescue assets and coordinate with VDOT on road monitoring
3
Issue Everbridge notifications to flood-prone areas if warranted
4
Initiate evacuation of threatened areas; open shelters as needed
Special considerations
Flooding is the highest-risk hazard for Botetourt County. Flash flooding in mountain valleys can occur rapidly with minimal warning time. Low-water crossings throughout the county are frequent flood hazard points.
Winter Storm / Ice Storm · EOP 10.2
Lead agency
Department of Fire & EMS (Coordinator of Emergency Management); VDOT (road operations).
Trigger conditions
National Weather Service issues Winter Storm Warning, or Ice Storm Warning for Botetourt County; forecast of significant snow accumulation, ice accumulation, or extended below-freezing temperatures.
Lifelines most impacted
Energy (power outages from ice/wind on lines); Transportation (road closures, hazardous travel); Health and Medical (EMS access delays); Safety and Security (increased service calls).
Key initial actions
1
Activate EOC monitoring; coordinate with NWS Blacksburg for forecast updates
2
Coordinate with VDOT
3
Alert utility providers (AEP, Craig-Botetourt Electric Co-op) for potential outage response
4
Prepare warming centers and check on vulnerable populations
5
Pre-position emergency supplies and generator assets
6
Issue public notifications regarding storm preparation and travel advisories
Special considerations
Elevation variance of over 3,000 feet across the county causes significant differences in precipitation type and accumulation. Ice storms cause the most prolonged power outages. Mountain roads may be impassable before valley roads are impacted. Extended cold without power is life-threatening to elderly and medically vulnerable populations.
Severe Weather (Tornado, Wind, Thunderstorm) · EOP 10.3
Lead agency
Department of Fire & EMS (rescue, EMS, damage assessment); Sheriff's Office (security, traffic control).
Trigger conditions
National Weather Service issues Severe Thunderstorm Warning or Tornado Warning for Botetourt County area; reports of damaging winds, large hail, or tornado touchdowns.
Lifelines most impacted
Safety and Security (rescue operations, structural damage); Energy (power outages); Transportation (debris on roadways); Communications (tower/line damage).
Key initial actions
1
Activate the PSAP for enhanced monitoring and dispatch; coordinate with Emergency Communications for radio system readiness
2
Issue Everbridge warnings for tornado warnings targeting affected areas
3
Deploy search and rescue teams to areas of reported damage
4
Coordinate damage assessment as conditions allow
5
Activate mutual aid for widespread damage
6
Open shelters for displaced residents

Derecho events, such as the June 2012 regional derecho, can cause widespread wind damage across the entire county. Tornadoes in the Roanoke Valley region are infrequent but have occurred. Severe thunderstorms with damaging winds are the most common warm-season severe weather threat. Mountain terrain may funnel winds and create localized damage patterns.

Department of Fire & EMS (structural protection); Virginia Department of Forestry (wildland fire suppression).
Trigger conditions

Lead agency
Department of Fire & EMS (Coordinator of Emergency Management).
Trigger conditions
National Hurricane Center forecast track indicates tropical storm or hurricane conditions likely for western Virginia; NWS issues Tropical Storm or Hurricane Warning; significant rainfall forecast from tropical system.
Lifelines most impacted
Transportation (flooding, debris, wind damage); Energy (prolonged power outages); Safety and Security (flooding, rescue); Food, Water, Shelter (displacement); Water Systems (water contamination, treatment plant damage).

Primary risk from tropical systems is flooding from heavy rainfall, not wind. Hurricane Helene (2024) demonstrated significant regional impacts from tropical remnants. Compound hazards (flooding, wind, power outage) may strain resources simultaneously.

Earthquake felt in Botetourt County as confirmed by USGS; reports of structural damage; Virginia Tech Seismological Observatory confirms significant seismic event in the region.

Building stock is generally not designed for seismic forces, increasing vulnerability.

Field guide · EOP 11.5.8
MCI position checklists
Botetourt County EOP 2026 Rev. 2 · Sections 11.5.8 and 11.5.9
Don the vest, set up your area, and work your checklist in order. Complete each step before moving to the next; do not skip steps without documenting why.
Vest colors
RedWhiteBlueTealPurpleYellowGreenBlackGray
Incident Commander (IC) · Red vest · 16 steps
Works for: Unified Command or independent command
Objective. Coordinate the overall incident response to save lives, stabilize the incident, protect property, and ensure rescuer safety. EMS will not typically command a major incident — transfer command to the most qualified officer as soon as practical.
1
Don RED Incident Commander vest.
2
Announce assumption of command on radio with your location.
3
Establish Command Post in a safe location with a clear view of the incident area. Use vehicle mobile radio. DO NOT self-deploy into the scene.
4
Transmit initial size-up to dispatch: (a) What happened and number of victims; (b) Potential hazards; (c) Resources on scene and their tasks; (d) Additional help needed.
5
Formally declare Mass Casualty Incident on radio. Specify MCI level (1-4) if determinable.
6
Request mutual aid EMS and fire resources consistent with MCI level via dispatch.
7
Develop initial strategy: (a) What must be done to make area safe; (b) Priorities for rescue and patient care; (c) Actions to prevent additional casualties.
8
Assign arriving resources to functional positions. Appoint first: Staging Area Manager, Safety Officer.
9
Assign or confirm Medical Group Supervisor (senior EMS officer on scene).
10
Appoint Safety Officer — instruct them to continuously monitor scene hazards.
11
Appoint Public Information Officer (PIO) or direct all media inquiries to dispatch/Emergency Manager.
12
Account for all personnel assigned to the incident throughout the event.
13
Coordinate with law enforcement for scene perimeter and security.
14
Authorize EOC activation for Level 1 and Level 2 incidents. Notify Emergency Manager.
15
Coordinate with Emergency Manager for public notification (Everbridge, media).
16
Perform clean handoff to successor: brief on incident status, resources committed/available/responding, strategy, and tasks in progress.
Safety Officer · White vest · 14 steps
Works for: Incident Commander
Objective. Identify and mitigate hazards that could cause injury or death to responders and patients. The Safety Officer has the authority to immediately stop any unsafe operation.
1
Don WHITE Safety Officer vest.
2
Report to Incident Commander and confirm assignment.
3
Conduct immediate 360-degree hazard assessment of the incident scene.
4
Identify and communicate hazards: fire, flammables, electrical, hazmat, structural instability, traffic, crowd, active threat.
5
Establish safe approach and egress routes for responders and communicate to all units.
6
Confirm proper PPE is worn by all responders for identified hazards.
7
Monitor weather conditions and communicate any hazards (lightning, high winds, temperature extremes).
8
Monitor responder fatigue. Request Rehabilitation as needed. Coordinate with Ambulance Staging Manager.
9
Continuously monitor for new or changing hazards throughout the incident.
10
Immediately halt any operation presenting imminent danger to life — notify IC.
11
Document all safety observations and corrective actions on Tactical Worksheet.
12
Brief IC on safety status at regular intervals.
13
Confirm Landing Zone safety for air medical operations if applicable.
14
Assist IC with After-Action documentation of safety findings.
Medical Group Supervisor · Blue vest · 19 steps
Works for: Operations Section Chief or IC (if no Operations)
Objective. Manage all Medical Group functions — extrication, triage, treatment, and transportation — to safely and efficiently care for all patients consistent with incident medical objectives.
1
Don BLUE Medical Group Supervisor vest.
2
Set up Medical Group Command Post where you are visible with a clear view of the working area.
3
Receive briefing from IC on incident objectives and overall strategy.
4
Set Medical Group objectives and ensure all Unit Leaders understand them.
5
Begin using Tactical Worksheets immediately to record key information.
6
Confirm Staging and traffic flow are established for arriving resources. Coordinate with Operations or IC.
7
Assign personnel to functional positions in this order: (1) Staging, Extrication, Triage; (2) Treatment; (3) Transportation; (4) Medical Communications.
8
Ensure each position leader dons appropriate vest and initiates checklist.
9
Request additional resources as needed. Keep unassigned resources in Staging.
10
Confirm Triage Unit Leader is established and START triage is underway.
11
Confirm Treatment Unit Leader is established and Treatment Area is set up and marked.
12
Confirm Transportation Unit Leader is established and hospital contact has been initiated.
13
Confirm Medical Communications Manager has established contact with Command Hospital or RHCC.
14
Monitor work and progress toward medical objectives continuously.
15
Monitor personnel condition — request relief crews to prevent fatigue-related errors.
16
Account for all assigned Medical Group personnel throughout the incident.
17
Maintain regular communication with IC/Operations on patient count, resource needs, and progress.
18
Authorize demobilization of Medical Group resources when patients are cleared.
19
Complete After-Action documentation for Medical Group operations.
Triage Unit Leader · Teal vest · 17 steps
Works for: Medical Group Supervisor
Objective. Locate, assess, and sort all patients to establish treatment priorities. Move patients to the Treatment Area and ensure deceased are properly managed.
1
Don TEAL Triage Unit Leader vest.
2
Set up Triage at the incident site or closest safe area if site is unsafe. Position where you are visible and have a clear view of the scene.
3
Report to Medical Group Supervisor and confirm assignment.
4
Immediately identify a safe holding area for GREEN (walking wounded) patients and broadcast on radio. Direct ambulatory patients there now.
5
Identify and dispatch Triage Teams to begin START. Direct teams to work through scene systematically. Subdivide scene into sectors and assign teams to each sector as needed.
6
Confirm all Triage Team members are using the START algorithm and applying colored surveyor tape (NOT triage tags — tags applied in Treatment).
7
Establish Porter Teams. Obtain stretchers, soft stretchers, backboards and straps from Staging or Medical Supply for Porter Teams.
8
Direct Porter Teams to follow Triage Teams: move REDs first, then YELLOWs to Treatment Area. Do not delay porter movement waiting only for REDs if YELLOWs are ready.
9
Designate a Fatality Manager. Direct them to log GREY patient locations and descriptions on Tactical Worksheet.
10
Confirm no GREY patients are moved without Medical Examiner approval (except to protect remains or to access living patients).
11
Conduct initial patient count by color category. Report count to Medical Group Supervisor.
12
Monitor Triage Team progress across the entire scene. Confirm all areas have been covered.
13
Request additional Triage Teams from Medical Group as scene size warrants.
14
Monitor condition of Triage personnel. Request relief crews as needed.
15
Account for all personnel assigned to Triage.
16
Keep Medical Group Supervisor, Extrication, and Treatment informed of patient counts and progress.
17
Notify Medical Group when primary triage of entire scene is complete.
Fatality Manager · Purple vest · 12 steps
Works for: Triage Unit Leader
Objective. Locate and safeguard the remains of the deceased and their personal effects pending arrival of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME).
1
Don PURPLE Fatality Manager vest.
2
Report to Triage Unit Leader and confirm assignment.
3
Locate and tag all deceased (GREY) victims in the incident area. Log approximate position on Tactical Worksheet with description of remains.
4
Establish a separate, secured GREY area distinct from the Treatment Area. Area must be accessible by 2-wheel-drive vehicles.
5
Request law enforcement to secure the GREY area. Do not use EMS providers to guard remains.
6
Coordinate with Treatment Unit and Triage to porter any patients who die in Treatment to the GREY area.
7
Maintain records of all patients dying in Treatment: identity if known, triage tag number, time and circumstances of death, description of clothing and personal effects.
8
Safeguard remains and personal effects. Do not leave remains unattended.
9
Where appropriate to preserve privacy or protect remains, cover with disposable non-absorbent sheets.
10
Do not authorize removal of any GREY patient prior to OCME approval (except to protect remains or to access living patients).
11
Keep Triage Unit Leader and Treatment Unit Leader informed of deceased count.
12
Transfer responsibility for all remains to the OCME representative upon arrival. Provide complete Tactical Worksheet documentation.
Treatment Unit Leader · Yellow vest · 19 steps
Works for: Medical Group Supervisor
Objective. Continually assess and stabilize patients and provide definitive pre-hospital treatment based on triage priority. Determine patient transport order.
1
Don YELLOW Treatment Unit Leader vest.
2
Select and establish the Treatment Area. Consider: (1) Safety; (2) Portering distance from scene; (3) Adequate space with room to expand; (4) Weather and temperature; (5) Lighting for night operations; (6) Ambulance access for Transportation Unit.
3
Mark the Treatment Area with color-coded flags, tarps, or chemlights: RED area, YELLOW area, GREEN area, and separate GREY area.
4
Notify Triage Unit Leader and Medical Group Supervisor of Treatment Area location.
5
Assign a Secondary Triage Officer at the entry point. Funnel all arriving patients through Secondary Triage before placement in treatment areas.
6
Apply Virginia Triage Tags (VDH-approved) to all patients at Secondary Triage.
7
Arrange Treatment Area in parallel rows with RED and YELLOW areas able to expand outward. Consider a separate location for GREEN patients if space permits.
8
Assign RED Area Manager, YELLOW Area Manager, and GREEN Area Manager. Each manager is responsible for their section.
9
Assign Medical Supply Manager. Direct them to set up Medical Supply adjacent to Treatment Area.
10
Staff Treatment teams per ratios: RED (1 ALS + 1 BLS per patient); YELLOW (1 BLS/patient + 1 ALS/3 patients); GREEN (1 BLS/3 patients).
11
Consider Special Procedures Teams for common interventions (airway management, IV access, hemorrhage control, splinting) if resources allow.
12
Supervise prehospital care per approved Virginia EMS protocols.
13
Continuously supervise re-triage of all patients in the Treatment Area.
14
Isolate emotionally disturbed patients from the main Treatment Area if possible.
15
Determine patient transport order in coordination with Transportation Unit Leader: RED first, then YELLOW, then GREEN.
16
Coordinate with Fatality Manager for patients who die in Treatment.
17
Monitor Treatment personnel condition. Request relief crews as needed.
18
Account for all assigned Treatment personnel.
19
Keep Medical Group Supervisor and Transportation Unit Leader continuously informed.
Medical Supply Manager · Purple vest · 10 steps
Works for: Treatment Unit Leader
Objective. Provide all supplies and equipment needed by Porter Teams and Treatment Area personnel to move and treat patients.
1
Don PURPLE Medical Supply Manager vest.
2
Set up Medical Supply immediately adjacent to and within easy reach of the Treatment Unit.
3
Contact Ambulance Staging Manager: request crews bring EXTRA supplies from staged vehicles to Medical Supply. Keep essential equipment on vehicles. Request: backboards and rescue baskets and straps; splints and bandages; oxygen equipment and airway kits (BVMs, NPA/OPA, suction); IV sets and fluid bags; bleeding control supplies (tourniquets, hemostatic gauze, pressure bandages); pre-packed disaster kits if available.
4
Sort all incoming supplies and arrange for rapid access by Treatment teams.
5
Establish inventory reorder points for critical supplies. Know when to request resupply.
6
For night operations: coordinate with Medical Group Supervisor and Ambulance Staging to bring portable lighting to Treatment Area.
7
Issue supplies as requested by Treatment teams. Track what is issued.
8
Contact Transportation Unit Leader to arrange for returning ambulances to bring additional supplies when reorder points are reached.
9
On completion: collect unused supplies and equipment. Return marked items to owning agencies. Arrange return or distribution of unmarked supplies.
10
Document all supply usage for After-Action and financial reimbursement purposes.
Transportation Unit Leader · Green vest · 17 steps
Works for: Medical Group Supervisor
Objective. Coordinate all patient transportation and maintain complete records of patient and unit movements.
1
Don GREEN Transportation Unit Leader vest.
2
Set up Transportation Unit at exit of Treatment Area with clear road access for ambulances.
3
Appoint as needed: Ambulance Staging Manager, Medical Communications Manager, Transport Recorder(s), Transport Loader(s), Air Ambulance Coordinator.
4
Establish vehicle flow: Ambulance Staging to Transportation Unit to Hospitals. Communicate route to all units.
5
Contact Command Hospital through Medical Communications Manager to determine hospital capacity in each triage category (RED/YELLOW/GREEN).
6
Select mode of transportation for each patient based on needs and available resources (ground ALS, BLS, air medical).
7
Order ambulances from Ambulance Staging as patients are ready in Treatment Area.
8
Load ambulances: RED patients first, then YELLOW, then GREEN. Mixed patient loads may be approved depending on hospital capacity.
9
If non-ambulance transport (bus, van) is available early, use for GREEN patients.
10
Ensure ambulances park parallel to each other. Avoid end-to-end parking. If end-to-end is unavoidable, load the first in line first.
11
Request Porter Teams from Triage to move patients from Treatment Area to ambulances.
12
Coordinate patient destinations with Command Hospital for each dispatched ambulance.
13
Brief ambulance crews before departure: destination hospital, route if non-standard, patient count, and any special considerations.
14
Record all patient and unit movements on Tactical Worksheet.
15
Monitor total patients transported, remaining in Treatment, and unaccounted for.
16
Keep Medical Group Supervisor and Treatment Unit Leader continuously informed.
17
Coordinate with returning ambulances to bring additional medical supplies to Medical Supply Manager.
Ambulance Staging Manager · Black vest · 14 steps
Works for: Transportation Unit Leader (may be co-located with incident Staging)
Objective. Maintain EMS manpower and ground vehicle resources ready for immediate dispatch at a location separated from the incident.
1
Don BLACK Ambulance Staging Manager vest.
2
Establish Ambulance Staging in coordination with Operations or incident Staging Manager. Select a site that is: away from the active scene; large enough for all needed units; easy road access from major routes; easy egress to Transportation Unit.
3
Use pull-through (parallel) staging arrangement whenever space permits. NOT end-to-end.
4
Direct all arriving ambulances and EMS vehicles to Staging.
5
Ensure all personnel on staged vehicles remain with their unit.
6
Park vehicles used to transport scene staff separately, out of the traffic flow.
7
Report available vehicle and personnel count to Transportation Unit Leader. Update continuously.
8
Ensure ambulance cots are NOT removed from vehicles (keep for transport).
9
As directed, remove extra supplies from ambulances for relocation to Medical Supply: backboards and straps, splints and bandages, blankets, portable oxygen and airway equipment, IV sets.
10
Coordinate Rehabilitation (food, drink, rest) for staged crews. Report crew welfare concerns to Safety Officer.
11
Dispatch vehicles to Transportation Unit only when ordered by Transportation Unit Leader.
12
Track status, number, and type of all ambulances in Staging on Tactical Worksheet.
13
Notify Transportation Unit Leader of any unit that becomes unavailable (mechanical failure, crew injury, etc.).
14
Coordinate with Mutual Aid Staging Officer if a separate incident Staging is established.
Medical Communications Manager · Gray vest · 12 steps
Works for: Transportation Unit Leader
Objective. Establish and maintain medical communications between the scene, Command Hospital, and RHCC. Serve as the primary interface for patient destination decisions.
1
Don GRAY Medical Communications Manager vest.
2
Set up at or adjacent to the Transportation Unit. Verify radio contact with the repeater or simplex channels in use.
3
Establish initial communications with Command Hospital (or nearest receiving hospital) using public safety radio, cellular, or amateur radio if available.
4
Break out Tactical Worksheets and use to track all communications and patient movement information.
5
Get initial information from Medical Group Supervisor. Provide Command Hospital with initial report — be accurate, identify estimates, do NOT speculate. Include: MCI Level/Category, cause of incident, number of patients by triage category, severity and types of injuries.
6
Get hospital emergency capacity information for each triage category. Relay to Transportation Unit Leader and Medical Group Supervisor.
7
For Level 1 and Level 2 incidents, contact NSPA RHCC at 1-866-679-7422. Provide: entity (Botetourt County), callback number, radio channel, MCI level and triage count, needs (patient placement or resources), hospitals already contacted, actions taken, incident summary.
8
Coordinate with Command Hospital or RHCC to determine destination for each dispatched ambulance.
9
Provide transport report to Command Hospital on each ambulance departure: transporting unit, destination hospital, number of patients, triage category, chief complaint, age, sex.
10
Monitor communications equipment status. Replace radio batteries as needed.
11
Maintain record of all hospitals contacted and their current capacity on Tactical Worksheet.
12
Keep Transportation Unit Leader and Medical Group Supervisor continuously informed.
Transport Recorder · Vest as assigned · 10 steps
Works for: Transportation Unit Leader
Objective. Ensure complete and accurate documentation of all patient and vehicle movements from scene to receiving hospitals.
1
Report to Transportation Unit Leader and receive Tactical Worksheets.
2
Set up at the patient loading point in the Transportation Area.
3
Record all patient movement information on Tactical Worksheet as each patient is loaded.
4
For every patient leaving Treatment, record and provide to Medical Communications Manager: (a) Transporting unit; (b) Destination hospital; (c) Number of patients on unit; (d) Patient information: triage category, age, sex, chief complaint; (e) ETA at destination.
5
Document Virginia Triage Tag numbers against each transported patient.
6
Maintain a running total of patients transported, by triage category.
7
Pass any additional patient information (special needs, family contact) to Medical Communications Manager for relay to receiving hospitals.
8
Maintain continuous communication with Transport Loaders to ensure all departures are captured.
9
Brief Transportation Unit Leader on transport status at regular intervals.
10
Compile final patient transport log for After-Action documentation.
Air Ambulance Coordinator · Vest as assigned · 12 steps
Works for: Transportation Unit Leader
Objective. Establish a safe helicopter Landing Zone (LZ) and coordinate all air medical operations into and out of the LZ.
1
Report to Transportation Unit Leader and confirm activation of air medical resources.
2
Select Landing Zone site. Minimum dimensions: Small helicopter: 60 ft x 60 ft (day) / 100 ft x 100 ft (night) | Medium helicopter: 75 ft x 75 ft (day) / 125 ft x 125 ft (night) | Large helicopter: 125 ft x 125 ft (day) / 200 ft x 200 ft (night).
3
LZ requirements: flat and firm surface free of debris; NOT adjacent to Treatment Area; clear approach path; upwind of any hazmat zone.
4
Assign personnel to assist in establishing and securing the LZ perimeter.
5
Mark the LZ. Preferred: cones, light sticks, or floodlights. Use flares ONLY if no ignition risk. At night: do NOT point spotlights, vehicle headlights, or white lights toward the aircraft.
6
Establish radio contact with inbound aircraft. Provide: obstructions (towers, power lines, buildings); wind direction and gusting conditions; special hazards; LZ GPS coordinates if requested.
7
Brief Transportation Unit Leader on LZ location, status, and aircraft ETA.
8
Coordinate patient loading and movement with Transportation Unit Leader.
9
CRITICAL: Maintain LZ safety. NO ONE approaches the aircraft who is not accompanied by a flight crew member.
10
After each aircraft departure, reset LZ for next inbound aircraft.
11
Report all air medical transports (unit, patient count, destination, ETA) to Transport Recorder.
12
Keep Transportation Unit Leader and Medical Communications Manager informed throughout all air operations.
Demobilization — All Positions · 14 steps
Sequence: Medical Group to Transportation to Treatment to Triage to Staging
Objective. Ensure an orderly stand-down that accounts for all personnel, equipment, and patients before releasing resources.
1
Confirm all patients have been transported or are accounted for (including deceased).
2
Medical Supply Manager: collect all unused supplies and equipment. Return marked items to owning agencies.
3
Medical Communications Manager: confirm all hospitals have final patient count and triage category breakdown. Close communications with RHCC if activated.
4
Transport Recorder: finalize patient transport log. Provide completed documentation to Medical Group Supervisor.
5
Fatality Manager: confirm transfer of responsibility for all remains to OCME. Provide complete documentation.
6
All Unit Leaders: account for all assigned personnel before releasing.
7
All Unit Leaders: collect completed Tactical Worksheets and provide to Medical Group Supervisor.
8
Medical Group Supervisor: compile Medical Group documentation. Provide complete package to IC.
9
Ambulance Staging Manager: release mutual aid units first after accounting. Notify owning agencies.
10
IC: prepare and submit After-Action Report (AAR) within 30 days.
11
Emergency Manager: schedule AAR meeting with all participating agencies within 14 days.
12
Complete VDEM incident report as required. Notify RHCC of MCI conclusion if they were activated.
13
Evaluate activation of Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) resources for responders.
14
Return all vests, equipment, and Tactical Worksheets to emergency management for inventory.

Just called in?
Never worked in an EOC before? This page is your first 15 minutes. Read it top to bottom. New words are explained in Words we use.
1
Confirm where to report
Most EOC activations are virtual. If you were not told whether to come in person, call the EOC line: 540-928-2265. If you go in person, bring your phone and charger, laptop, ID and a notebook.
2
Check in with the EOC Manager
The Coordinator of Emergency Management runs the EOC. Tell them your name, your agency and the role you are filling. They will confirm your job and the next briefing time.
3
Get the picture
Read the Now strip at the top of this page: the incident, EOC status, operational period and when the next report is due. Then read the latest situation report.
4
Find your role
Each role card says what your job is, what to do first and which pages and checklist are yours.
Who are you?
5
Work your checklist
Open your checklist and mark tasks as you finish them. The EOC sees your progress live.
6
Report up, on time
Before each briefing, give your status and what changed to the Planning Section. If something gets worse, such as a lifeline turning red, tell the EOC Manager right away. Do not wait for the briefing.
7
Write it down
Keep a log with times: decisions, calls, requests and who you talked to. Track your hours and any costs for Finance. FEMA and state reimbursement depend on these records.
Ground rules
•
Life safety comes first. If someone is in danger, call 9-1-1.
•
Ask through the EOC. Request people, equipment and supplies through Logistics, not on your own.
•
One voice to the public. Only the PIO releases information. Do not post about the incident.
•
Not sure? Ask. The EOC Manager would rather answer a question than fix a mistake.

Field guide · start here
Words we use
Plain-language meanings for the terms you will hear in the EOC.
EOC
Emergency Operations Center
Where county leaders coordinate the response: information, resources and decisions. It supports the people in the field; it does not direct them on scene. Most activations are virtual.
Activation level
Level 3, 2, 1
How big the EOC response is. Level 3 is the smallest. Level 1 is full activation, with all lifeline leads taking part.
Steady state
No active incident
Normal days. The EOC is not activated; this is when plans, training and contact lists get updated.
ICS
Incident Command System
The standard way every agency organizes a response: Command, Operations, Planning, Logistics and Finance/Admin. The same structure works at a house fire or a hurricane.
Incident Commander
IC
The person in charge at the scene. The EOC supports the IC.
Operational period
Op period
The block of time the current plan covers, often 12 hours. Each one starts with a briefing.
Briefing
A short meeting at the start of each operational period: what changed, what we are doing next, who does what.
SitRep
Situation report
The written snapshot of what is happening right now. Planning writes it; it goes to county leaders and VDEM.
IAP
Incident Action Plan
The goals and assignments for the next operational period.
Community lifelines
The 8 essential services
Safety & Security; Food, Water, Shelter; Health & Medical; Energy; Communications; Transportation; Hazardous Materials; Water Systems. We measure how the community is doing by checking each one.
Stabilized / Impacted / Destabilized
Green / yellow / red
A lifeline's status. Green: working normally. Yellow: working with workarounds or at risk. Red: failed or severely disrupted, needs priority help.
Lifeline lead
Lead agency
The department or partner responsible for reporting on a lifeline and working its checklist.
ESF
Emergency Support Function
The state and federal way of grouping support (for example ESF-6, Mass Care). Botetourt organizes its plan by lifelines instead.
Mutual aid
Help borrowed from other localities under signed agreements: people, equipment or supplies.
Resource request
213RR
A formal request for something the response needs. It goes through Logistics so nothing is ordered twice.
Local emergency declaration
A formal declaration by the Board of Supervisors. It unlocks emergency powers and is needed for state and federal aid.
VDEM
Virginia Department of Emergency Management
The state emergency management agency. Botetourt is in VDEM Region 6.
Damage assessment
IDA / PDA
Counting damaged homes and public property after a disaster. The totals decide whether the county qualifies for aid.
Public / Individual Assistance
PA / IA
FEMA programs. PA repays governments for response and repair costs. IA helps households.
Cost code
A number given to each event so every hour, purchase and piece of equipment can be tracked for reimbursement.
POD
Point of Distribution
A site where the public picks up water, food or supplies.
Shelter
A safe place for people who cannot stay home, often with Red Cross and Social Services.
FAC
Family Assistance Center
A place where families get information and support after a mass-casualty incident.
MCI
Mass-casualty incident
More patients than local EMS can normally handle at once.
PIO / JIC
Public Information Officer / Joint Information Center
The PIO is the one voice to the public and media. A JIC is when several agencies' PIOs work together.
Everbridge
The county's mass-notification system for alerts by phone, text and email.
AFN
Access and functional needs
People who need extra help in an emergency, such as those with disabilities, medical devices or no transportation.
Situational awareness
Knowing what is happening, where, and what it means. The SitRep, map and lifeline status are how the EOC keeps it.

What's due when
The EOC works in a repeating cycle called the operational period, often 12 hours. The EOC Manager sets the exact times for each event.
1 · Start of each operational period
Operational briefing
The EOC Manager runs it. The Director sets priorities. Each role gives a one-minute status. Leave knowing your assignments.
2 · During the period
Work and update
Work your checklist. Change your lifeline status as soon as it changes, not just at briefing time. Log decisions, calls and costs.
3 · About 1 hour before the SitRep is due
Lifeline reports to Planning
Each lifeline lead sends status (green, yellow or red), what changed and what they need.
4 · SitRep due time
Planning publishes the SitRep
It goes to county leaders and VDEM Region 6. The Now strip shows when the next one is due.
5 · Before the next period
Planning meeting
Section chiefs and the EOC Manager set objectives for the next Incident Action Plan.
6 · End of your shift
Hand off
Brief your replacement in person or by phone. Hand over your log and open items.
What to bring to a briefing
Lifeline lead
Status color, what changed, what you need, when you expect it to change.
Operations
Field situation and resources assigned.
Logistics
Resource requests: open, filled, delayed.
Planning
SitRep draft, lifeline summary, weather.
PIO
Messages sent, media and rumors to address.
Finance / Admin
Costs to date and anything needing approval.
Director
Priorities, policy decisions, declaration status.

A 10-minute orientation for anyone new, and a quarterly drill so the first time you use EM Watch is not during a real event.
10-minute orientation
  1. Open EM Watch on your phone and save it to your home screen.
  2. Read Just called in?
  3. Find your card on Who are you?
  4. Open your lifeline or role page and read the three questions at the top.
  5. Open your live checklist and see what it looks like.
  6. Read the latest SitRep.
  7. Save the EOC line in your phone: 540-928-2265.
Just called in?Who are you?
Quarterly drill · with the Everbridge test
Emergency Management: Send the quarterly Everbridge test and announce the drill.
Planning: Write a practice SitRep with the incident name EXERCISE. Mark it Final when the drill ends so EM Watch returns to steady state.
Lifeline leads: Open your page and checklist, and practice reporting your status to Planning. Do not check off real tasks.
Everyone: Confirm your phone number on Key contacts is right.
Emergency Management: After the drill: reset checklists, update contacts and set the next review date on any page that changed.
